title: Funerals in the code
hook: cremation, Kirtan Sohila and Ardas, a reading of the Granth, and no monuments

segments.voice: Yesterday, the code's quiet permission: a widow or widower may marry again, if they wish, with the same four rounds. Your line was starting over allowed. What plain thing did you do for someone beginning again? Day one thousand two hundred seventy.

There's a prayer Sikhs say at night, just before sleep. It's called Kirtan Sohila, and it's short, and in some homes children grow up hearing it at bedtime, lights low, the day being put away. Now the same words, in a different place. A crematorium, or an open pyre. A family standing close together. The body has been bathed and dressed. And the same bedtime prayer is said over it. The words that close an ordinary day are the words that close a life. That one choice says a great deal about how the Sikh code asks people to say goodbye.
screen: `A PRAYER BEFORE SLEEP.` → `THE SAME WORDS AT THE PYRE.` → `CLOSING A DAY, CLOSING A LIFE.`

segments.voice: The Sikh Rehat Maryada lays out a funeral in a few plain steps. In paraphrase: the body is bathed and clothed, and if the person was initiated, the five articles of faith stay with them. The body is cremated; where cremation isn't possible, the code allows other means. On the way and at the pyre, hymns are sung, Kirtan Sohila is recited when the fire is lit, and Ardas is said. Then a reading of the Guru Granth Sahib is begun, at home or in a gurdwara, and when it's complete there's a bhog, the closing we met not long ago. Notice what the code leaves out. It discourages loud wailing and breast-beating, and it rejects rituals that grew up around death outside the Guru's teaching. And it asks that no monument be built over the place where the body was cremated. Why so plain? Because in Sikh teaching a death happens within the hukam, God's order, the same order that gave the life. Grief is real, and the Gurus wrote about it; but the goodbye turns the family toward the Word instead of toward a stone. The ashes are not enshrined. The reading of the Granth is the memorial. That's what makes Kirtan Sohila fit. It's the prayer of going to rest, of a day returned to the One who gave it. Said at the pyre, it treats death as the last evening, met with the same words as every other. A simple goodbye isn't a cold one. It's a goodbye with nothing standing between the mourners and the Guru.
screen: `BATHED, CLOTHED, CREMATED.` · `KIRTAN SOHILA AND ARDAS.` · `A READING OF THE GRANTH, NO MONUMENT.` · `A DEATH WITHIN THE HUKAM.` · then, large: `SIMPLE GOODBYES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: think of a simple goodbye. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone who has died, or someone you've had to let go of. Don't relive the whole story. Ask only this: if the goodbye were as plain as the code's, what few words would be enough? Maybe a single line, maybe only their name, said once. Hold those words until the bell. If you pray, you can say Waheguru once for them. If the memory is heavy, it's fine to stop and simply breathe. The bell holds the time.
Funerals in the code. Cremation, Kirtan Sohila and Ardas at the pyre, a reading of the Guru Granth Sahib, and no monument. Today's word.
Your line: simple goodbyes. Today, when you part from someone, skip the long sign-off: one plain goodbye, said warmly, and let it be enough. Day one thousand two hundred seventy.

howItsDone: At a Sikh funeral the body is bathed, dressed and cremated while hymns are sung; Kirtan Sohila and Ardas are recited, a reading of the Guru Granth Sahib follows, and no monument is raised where the body was cremated.
